beats.text: Before cinema, before art, there was the eye. It began as almost nothing: a patch of light-sensitive cells that could tell day from night. Fold that patch into a cup, and it can tell where the light is coming from. Narrow the cup into a pinhole, and an image appears. Fill it with a lens, and the image sharpens. In 1994, the biologists Dan-Eric Nilsson and Susanne Pelger estimated that this could happen in fewer than four hundred thousand generations. In the history of life, that's a blink.

beats.text: Your eyes are fish eyes. Around five hundred million years ago, early jawless fish already had camera eyes, with a lens, a retina, and muscles to aim them. We inherited the design, flaws included. Our retina is wired backwards: its nerves run in front of the light-sensitive cells, and where they leave the eye there's a hole, the blind spot. Fish, reptiles and birds have four kinds of color cells. Our mammal ancestors, living at night in the age of the dinosaurs, lost two. Our primate ancestors won one back. That's why you see the colors you see.

beats.text: Philosophers were worried about seeing long before cinema. Around 375 BC, Plato imagined prisoners chained in a cave, facing a wall. Behind them burns a fire, and people carry objects past it, so the prisoners see only shadows. They take the shadows for the world. It's the oldest description of a movie theater, and a warning: what you see may be a projection.

beats.text: Around 1790, the poet William Blake wrote that if the doors of perception were cleansed, everything would appear as it is: infinite. In 1953, the writer Aldous Huxley took mescaline with the psychiatrist Humphry Osmond, and borrowed Blake's phrase for a book: The Doors of Perception. A few years later, Osmond proposed a new word for drugs that seemed to reveal the mind. Psychedelic. From the Greek: mind-manifesting.

beats.text: In 1637, René Descartes described cutting away the back of an ox's eye, and seeing the world projected on it, small and upside down. But that raised a puzzle. If the eye makes a picture, who looks at the picture? A little person inside the head? Then who looks inside that little person's head? Philosophers call it an infinite regress, and it looks a lot like video feedback. Today, many neuroscientists say the brain doesn't watch a picture at all: it predicts one, and checks its guess against the light. Perception, in their phrase, is a controlled hallucination. Which brings us to the machines.
